summary: This Wikipedia article explains the poverty threshold (poverty line), the minimum income deemed adequate in a particular country, usually calculated from the annual cost of necessities for an average adult, with housing as the largest component. It covers the history of the concept from Charles Booth and Seebohm Rowntree through Mollie Orshansky, the absolute poverty measures set by the World Bank (International Poverty Line), the basic needs approach, and the relative poverty concept. The excerpt is cut off partway through the relative poverty comparison section; the note also contains a banner stating the article focuses mainly on the United States.
one_line: Wikipedia article on the poverty threshold, the minimum income deemed adequate in a country, covering its history, absolute and relative measures.
key_facts: The poverty threshold, poverty limit, poverty line, or breadline is the minimum level of income deemed adequate in a particular country.
The poverty line is usually calculated by estimating the total cost of one year's worth of necessities for the average adult.
In September 2022, the World Bank updated the International Poverty Line to $2.15 per day in PPP.
As of 2022, the World Bank cited $3.65 per day in PPP for lower-middle income countries and $6.85 per day in PPP for upper-middle income countries.

Per the $1.90/day standard, the share of the global population in absolute poverty fell from over 80% in 1800 to 10% by 2015, according to United Nations estimates, which found roughly 734 million people remained in absolute poverty.
Charles Booth, a pioneering investigator of poverty in London at the turn of the 20th century, popularised the idea of a poverty line, a concept originally conceived by the London School Board.
Booth set the line at 10 (50p) to 20 shillings (£1) per week, which he considered the minimum necessary for a family of four or five people to subsist on.
Seebohm Rowntree surveyed families in York and concluded that 27.84% of the total population of York lived below his poverty line.
Mollie Orshansky first developed the poverty threshold between 1963 and 1964 by taking the cost of a food plan per family of three or four and multiplying it by a factor of three.
In 1969 the inter agency poverty level review committee adjusted the threshold for only price changes.
The basic needs approach was introduced by the International Labour Organization's World Employment Conference in 1976.
David Gordon's paper for the United Nations defines absolute poverty as the absence of any two of eight basic needs.
In 1967, Victor Fuchs proposed that "we define as poor any family whose income is less than one-half the median family income."

The threshold for relative poverty is considered to be at 50% of a country's median equivalised disposable income after social transfers, while the OECD and European Union main poverty line is set at 60% of median household income.
Adam Smith argued in 1776 that poverty is the inability to afford whatever the custom of the country renders it indecent for creditable people, even of the lowest order, to be without.
